newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia vows action after gangland cemetery bombing.
newsitem.headline: Russia vows action after gangland cemetery bombing.

text.p: Russian police have launched a major operation to track down gangland bombers that slaughtered 13 mourners at a Moscow cemetery on Sunday.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, underlining the threat organised crime poses to a society struggling with economic reform, demanded that the killers be brought to book.

The odds are stacked against the police, who rarely clear up gang murders. Yet the massacre, put down to crime clans linked to Afghan war veterans' groups, has managed to shock a nation where mafia killings have become commonplace in the chaotic five years since the collapse of communism.

The blast, which claimed the lives of the widow and mother of a veterans' leader who was himself blown up two years ago, is a stark reminder to President Boris Yeltsin of the problems he must face as he appears to be recovering well from open heart surgery.
"Everything has been set in motion to solve this crime, unprecedented in its audacity and its scale," Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said, describing the bombers as "scum".
Ominously for Kulikov, Chernomyrdin said the minister would be personally accountable for solving the cemetery slaying.
"This is a challenge...which cannot go unheeded," he said. "The minister...will draw the appropriate conclusions."
"They have thrown down the gauntlet. The challenge has been accepted," Kulikov defiantly told NTV television.

Among those killed at Kotlyakovskoye cemetery in south Moscow were the widow, mother and uncle of Mikhail Likhodei, a veterans' leader whose murder in a bomb blast on November 10, 1994, they were commemorating with some 130 fellow mourners.

The bomb, equivalent to between two and five kg (4-10 lb) of high explosive, went off under a table laden with food and drink for the gathering. Bodies were hurled across the graveyard in one of the most spectacularly gruesome killings Moscow has seen.

Also killed was Likhodei's successor as head of the Afghan War Invalids' Foundation. Police and veterans' leaders said the bomb was clearly a settling of scores among criminals associated with veterans groups, which benefit from generous tax breaks.
But by late on Sunday, there was no indication from the police that they had any firm leads to the bombers.

Yeltsin, who early in the day issued a Militia Day message saying he was sure the police were doing all they could to "strengthen the rule of law", is already easing himself back into affairs of state, his two daughters said on Sunday.

In an unusual appearance that underlined the sense of relief in Yeltsin's entourage at his speedy recovery, daughters Tatyana and Yelena confided about their fears before the operation to NTV and said the president was getting back to his old self.
"Every day he changes, he really looks better...even the expression in his eyes changes," said Yelena.
The 65-year-old president already had "a mountain of papers" on his desk but was following doctors' orders and refraining from overtaxing himself with meetings.
Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told Russian Television Yeltsin could move out of hospital to the state sanatorium at Barvikha, just outside Moscow, in eight to 10 days.
Among the most pressing tasks for Russia's rulers is the severe economic crisis, which has seen millions go unpaid for months, closing down businesses and prompting protests.

Chernomyrdin will chair a meeting of the Defence Council on Monday. High on the agenda is expected to be the setting of a timetable for paying back wages to servicemen and defence workers who have been among the hardest hit by the cash crunch.
